chapter_summary:
The User Interface (UI) is the player's primary means of interacting with your game and receiving crucial information. Whether it's a health bar, a score display, an inventory screen, or a main menu, a well-designed UI is essential for a smooth and enjoyable player experience. Unity's UI system is built around the `Canvas` component. A `Canvas` is a special `GameObject` that all UI elements must reside within. It renders UI elements on top of your game world, and you can configure how it scales and renders. The three main Render Modes for a `Canvas` are: "Screen Space - Overlay" (UI always on top, scales with screen size), "Screen Space - Camera" (UI rendered in front of a specific camera, scales with camera view), and "World Space" (UI exists as a 3D object in the game world, useful for in-world signs or interactive panels). For most game UIs like HUDs and menus, "Screen Space - Overlay" or "Screen Space - Camera" are the most common choices.

Within the `Canvas`, every UI element, from text to images to buttons, uses a `Rect Transform` component instead of a regular `Transform`. The `Rect Transform` is specifically designed for 2D UI layouts, allowing you to define the position, size, and anchoring of elements relative to their parent `Rect Transform` or the `Canvas` itself. Anchors are incredibly important for creating responsive UIs that adapt to different screen resolutions and aspect ratios. By setting an element's anchors (e.g., to the top-left, center, or stretching across the entire screen), you dictate how it will resize and reposition itself when the screen changes. For example, a score display might be anchored to the top-right corner, ensuring it always stays there regardless of screen size. A common mistake is to ignore anchors, leading to UIs that look great on one resolution but become distorted or misaligned on others. Always test your UI on multiple resolutions using the Game view's resolution dropdown.

Unity provides a rich set of built-in UI elements. `Text` is used to display strings of characters, often for scores, instructions, or dialogue. You can customize its font, size, color, alignment, and even add outlines or shadows. `Image` is used to display sprites or textures, perfect for health bars, character portraits, or decorative UI elements. `Button` is one of the most fundamental interactive elements. It combines an `Image` (for its visual appearance) with a `Button` component that handles click events. When you create a `Button`, you'll see an "On Click()" event list in its Inspector. Here, you can drag any `GameObject` from your scene that has a script with a public method, and then select that method to be called when the button is pressed. For instance, a "Start Game" button might call a `StartGame()` method on a `GameManager` script.

To organize multiple UI elements efficiently, Unity offers `Layout Group` components. These include `Horizontal Layout Group`, `Vertical Layout Group`, and `Grid Layout Group`. By adding a `Layout Group` to a parent `GameObject` (which also needs a `Rect Transform`), its child UI elements will automatically arrange themselves in a row, column, or grid, respectively. This is invaluable for creating dynamic lists, inventories, or menu options without manually positioning each item. For example, if you have a list of inventory slots, placing them inside a `Horizontal Layout Group` ensures they are evenly spaced and resize correctly. Building a simple in-game HUD involves combining these elements: a `Text` element for the score, an `Image` for a health bar (often filled dynamically by a script), and perhaps a `Button` to pause the game. These elements would all be children of your main `Canvas` and carefully positioned and anchored to ensure they remain visible and functional across various display settings.

screens.title: User Interface (UI) Design and Implementation
screens.subtitle: How Canvas, Rect Transform, anchors and UI elements create responsive in-game interfaces

narration.text: In this lesson you'll learn what makes a game interface both readable and robust across screen sizes. We begin with the Canvas, the container that renders all UI, then look at the Rect Transform which replaces Transform for 2D layout, and finally practical elements like Text, Image and Button. You'll see how anchors control responsiveness, how layout groups simplify repeated UI, and how a small C# manager updates score and health at runtime. A concrete example will guide you: building a heads-up display that uses TextMeshPro for a score and a filled Image for a health bar. I'll highlight a common mistake: leaving anchors at default so UI drifts on different resolutions, and a quick debugging tip: use the Game view resolution presets to test. By the end you'll understand the relationship between the Canvas render modes, how anchors map a child to its parent's rectangle, and how to wire a button to a public method. Think about one UI element you rely on in a favorite game — how should it behave when the window resizes?

keyIdea.title: UI is a layout + interaction system
keyIdea.text: Canvas holds UI, Rect Transform controls layout, and anchors plus layout groups make interfaces responsive and maintainable.

screens.title: Canvas and Render Modes
screens.subtitle: What the Canvas is and when to use each render mode

narration.text: The Canvas is the foundational GameObject for all Unity UI. It is a special renderer that controls how UI elements draw relative to cameras and the screen. There are three render modes you must know. Screen Space - Overlay places UI on top of the scene and always faces the player; it's the simplest choice for HUDs and menus because it scales with screen size and ignores world depth. Screen Space - Camera renders UI using a chosen camera so the UI can appear between layers or align with camera perspective; this is useful when you want the UI to feel tied to a particular view or to coexist with scene depth effects. World Space makes UI a regular 3D object in the scene: useful for in-world panels, floating labels, or interactive terminals that players can walk up to. A concrete example: for a HUD showing score and health use Screen Space - Overlay so those elements remain visible regardless of camera motion. A common misconception is to use World Space for everything because it looks 3D; that makes stable HUD placement harder and forces extra work to scale across resolutions. Key takeaway: pick the render mode based on whether the UI should always stay on screen or exist inside the world, then test with the Game view to confirm behavior. How would you decide for an in-world vending machine versus a pause menu?

keyIdea.title: Canvas chooses where UI lives
keyIdea.text: Overlay for HUDs and menus, Camera for view-aligned UI, World Space for interactive in-world panels.

content.html:
Core Concept
Canvas and Render Modes
Choose how UI is rendered relative to the screen and cameras.
  • Overlay: Always on top, scales with screen — ideal for HUDs and menus.
  • Camera: Renders in front of a specific camera — good for view-dependent UI.
  • World Space: UI as 3D objects — use for in-world panels and signs.
Example: HUD uses Overlay to remain visible.
Misconception: World Space equals better visuals — not for HUDs.
Annotated Cards
When to use Overlay
Health bars, score counters, and pause menus that must always be visible use Overlay for consistency and simplicity.
When to use Camera
Use Camera mode when UI should respect camera depth or when render order matters with scene objects.
When to use World Space
Use World Space for floating screens or interactable terminals that players can approach in the 3D world.

screens.title: Rect Transform and Anchors
screens.subtitle: Understanding position, size, pivot and anchors for responsive layout

narration.text: Rect Transform replaces the usual 3D Transform for UI elements and gives you controls tailored to 2D layout: anchored position, size delta, pivot, and four anchor points that define the element's rectangle relative to its parent. Anchors are the most important concept for responsive UI. When you set an element's anchors to a corner, its position remains relative to that corner even as screen size changes. When you stretch anchors across an area, the element resizes with the parent. A concrete example: anchor a score label to the top-right so it maintains a constant offset from that corner across phones and monitors. The pivot controls how rotations and scaling are applied relative to the element's local origin. A common mistake is leaving anchors centered with manual offsets; the UI will look right in one resolution and break in another. To debug, use the Rect Tool in the Editor and toggle anchor presets (Shift+Alt + preset) to see the resulting behavior. Key takeaway: set anchors deliberately to express how an element should move or resize, then use the Game view to confirm. What element in your UI should stretch versus remain fixed?

keyIdea.title: Anchors drive responsiveness
keyIdea.text: Anchors define how a UI element's rectangle relates to its parent and determine resizing and repositioning across resolutions.

content.html:
Definition
Rect Transform & Anchors
Anchors set where an element ties to its parent; pivot sets its local origin for transforms.
Anchored Position: Pixel offset from the anchor rectangle.
Size Delta: Width and height relative to anchors.
Pivot: The point used for rotation and scale inside the element.
Example: Top-right score stays anchored and readable.
Mistake: Leaving default center anchors causes drift on resize.
Practical Steps
  1. Select Rect Tool, pick an anchor preset that matches desired behavior.
  2. Use Shift+Alt with a preset to set both anchors and offsets quickly.
  3. Test by changing Game view resolution and observing repositioning.
Checklist: Did the element keep its offset? Did it stretch appropriately? If not, adjust anchors or switch to stretch anchors.

screens.title: Text, Image and Button Basics
screens.subtitle: Creating readable text, image-based bars, and interactive buttons

narration.text: Unity's built-in UI elements cover the most common interface needs. Text (or TextMeshPro recommended) displays strings with control over font, size, color and alignment; use TextMeshPro for sharper text and better styling. Image displays sprites or textures; it is the building block for decorative elements and functional controls like health bars. For a dynamic health bar, use two Image objects: a darker background and a fill child with Image Type set to Filled. The fill image supports a fillAmount that scripts can change between 0 and 1 to represent health. Buttons combine an Image and a Button component that exposes an On Click() event list you can populate in the Inspector. To wire a Start button to code, drag a GameObject with a public method into the slot and select the method. A concrete example: create a Button labeled "Start Game" that calls a public StartGame method on your GameManager. A common misunderstanding is that button clicks require code attached to the button object; instead, the button simply invokes public methods on any referenced GameObject. Key takeaway: pick TextMeshPro for clarity, use Images for filled bars, and use the Button's On Click to connect UI to gameplay logic. How would you design a restart button using this pattern?

keyIdea.title: Elements and interactions
keyIdea.text: TextMeshPro for clear text, Image for visuals and fill bars, Button uses On Click to call public methods.

content.html:
Core Component
Text, Image, Button
Use TextMeshPro for crisp labels, Image for visuals, Button for interaction.
TextMeshPro: import TMP Essentials if prompted, then add a TextMeshPro UGUI element.
Image Fill: child Image set to Filled and Horizontal allows script control via fillAmount.
Button: assign a public method to On Click() via Inspector.
Example Card
Create a Stop button that calls GameManager.PauseGame() by dragging the GameManager into the button's On Click slot and selecting the method.
Common mistake
Assuming a button must have a script on itself; instead it only triggers public methods on referenced objects.
Key Takeaway

Use Button's On Click to call public methods; keep logic in manager scripts, not on the button itself.

screens.title: Layout Groups for Organized UI
screens.subtitle: Use Horizontal, Vertical and Grid Layout Groups to automate arrangement

narration.text: Layout Groups remove manual positioning of repeated UI items by arranging children automatically. Choose a Horizontal Layout Group to line elements left-to-right, a Vertical Layout Group for columns, or a Grid Layout Group when you need rows and columns with uniform sizing. To use them, add the appropriate Layout Group component to a parent GameObject with a Rect Transform, then place child UI elements as children. Enable Content Size Fitter or use Layout Element to control individual child sizing when needed. A concrete example: an inventory bar uses a Horizontal Layout Group so new slots flow in without repositioning each item; spacing and padding settings control the gaps. A common mistake is to place non-UI objects or nested canvases inside a layout parent, which can break layout calculations. Another pitfall is relying on layout groups for pixel-perfect art placement — they are best for dynamic lists, not for decorative overlays needing precise pixel offsets. Key takeaway: layout groups save time and make your UI adapt to content changes; combine them with anchors to ensure they stay in the right place on screen. Which list in your game would benefit from a layout group?

keyIdea.title: Automate arrangement
keyIdea.text: Layout Groups automatically position and size child elements, ideal for inventories, menus, and dynamic lists.

content.html:
Process Flow
Layout Groups
Add a layout component to a parent to manage child positions automatically.
Horizontal: Arrange children in a row with spacing and padding.
Vertical: Stack children in a column; useful for menus.
Grid: Produce uniform cell grids for inventory or level selectors.
Example & Notes
Inventory example: parent GameObject has Horizontal Layout Group and child slots are Image objects. Adding slots automatically updates layout spacing.
Tip: combine Layout Element on a child to override min width or preferred height when one slot needs different sizing.
Common Mistake

Putting layout groups on objects that should not change size leads to jitter. Use them for dynamic content only.

screens.title: UIManager Script: Update Score and Health
screens.subtitle: A simple script to connect TextMeshPro and Image fill to gameplay values

narration.text: This walkthrough focuses on a compact UIManager script that demonstrates how UI elements are updated from code. The script exposes two public fields: one for a TextMeshProUGUI reference to show the score, and one for an Image reference used as the health bar fill. On Start it initializes values, and public methods UpdateScore and UpdateHealth set the visible score text and the health image's fillAmount. A concrete example in the chapter shows UpdateScore adding ten points when pressing P and UpdateHealth decreasing by 0.1 when pressing O. Why this design matters: it separates UI logic from gameplay systems and keeps references clear in the Inspector so designers can swap visuals without changing code. A common misconception is to search for UI objects at runtime using GameObject. Find; this is fragile. Instead, assign references in the Inspector or use dependency injection patterns. Closing question: how would you extend this script to animate the health bar change smoothly instead of jumping to the new fill amount? UIManager Script: Update Score and Health means keep public references for text and images and update them through simple public methods, avoiding runtime finds.. In practical terms, a simple script to connect textmeshpro and image fill to gameplay values. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Expose UI references
keyIdea.text: Keep public references for text and images and update them through simple public methods, avoiding runtime finds.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
UIManager.cs
This script shows public fields for the score text and health fill and methods to update them.
using UnityEngine;
using TMPro;
using UnityEngine.UI;

public class UIManager : MonoBehaviour
{
  public TextMeshProUGUI scoreText; // Drag your ScoreText here
  public Image healthBarFill;       // Drag your HealthBarFill here

  private int currentScore = 0;
  private float currentHealth = 1.0f; // 0.0 to 1.0

  void Start()
  {
    UpdateScore(0);
    UpdateHealth(1.0f);
  }

  public void UpdateScore(int newScore)
  {
    currentScore = newScore;
    if (scoreText != null)
      scoreText.text = "Score: " + currentScore;
  }

  public void UpdateHealth(float newHealthNormalized)
  {
    currentHealth = Mathf.Clamp01(newHealthNormalized);
    if (healthBarFill != null)
      healthBarFill.fillAmount = currentHealth;
  }

  void Update()
  {
    if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.P)) UpdateScore(currentScore + 10);
    if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.O)) UpdateHealth(currentHealth - 0.1f);
  }
}
Annotations
  • Public fields: Assign references in the Inspector to avoid fragile runtime lookups.
  • Update methods: Keep them simple and focused on UI representation only.
  • Clamp health: Use Mathf.Clamp01 to ensure fillAmount stays between 0 and 1.
Key Takeaway

Expose UI refs and update their visual properties from clear public methods; this keeps UI and game logic decoupled.

screens.title: Building the HUD: Step-by-step
screens.subtitle: Create Canvas, ScoreText, HealthBarBackground and HealthBarFill

narration.text: We'll build a simple HUD step-by-step so you can reproduce it in your project. Step one: create a Canvas from GameObject > UI > Canvas; this will also add an EventSystem. Choose Screen Space - Overlay for a typical HUD. Step two: add a TextMeshPro element and rename it ScoreText. Set its Rect Transform anchors to top-left using Shift+Alt presets, then change the text content to "Score: 0" and adjust font size. Step three: create an Image and rename it HealthBarBackground; position and anchor it to top-right. Add a child Image called HealthBarFill and set its Image Type to Filled with Horizontal method and Fill Origin Left. Set the fill image color to green and the background to a darker shade. Step four: create an empty GameObject called UIManager and attach the UIManager. cs script. In the Inspector drag ScoreText into the scoreText slot and HealthBarFill into healthBarFill slot. Finally, run the scene and press P and O to simulate changes. A common error is forgetting to set the child fill image type to Filled; without it scripts cannot control health visually. What will you test after connecting your UI to code?

keyIdea.title: Follow the HUD recipe
keyIdea.text: Create Canvas → Text → Background Image → Fill Image (Filled type) → Attach UIManager and wire references in Inspector.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity
Building a Simple HUD
1. Create Canvas
GameObject > UI > Canvas, choose Screen Space - Overlay. Ensure EventSystem exists.
2. Add ScoreText
Add TextMeshPro, set anchors to top-left (Shift+Alt preset), set text to "Score: 0" and adjust font size.
3. Health Bar
Create Image for background, child Image for fill. Set child to Filled, Horizontal, Fill Origin Left and color to green.
4. UIManager
Create UIManager object, attach script and drag ScoreText and HealthBarFill into their slots in Inspector.
Checklist & Tips
  • Set the fill image type to Filled or fillAmount won't work.
  • Assign references in Inspector instead of using GameObject.Find.
  • Test with Game view presets to validate anchors across resolutions.
Key Takeaway

Follow the sequence and verify anchor behavior early to prevent layout breakage later.

screens.title: Connecting UI to Scripts in the Inspector
screens.subtitle: How to expose and assign public fields so UI updates reliably

narration.text: The Inspector is how Unity bridges Editor objects to script fields. When you declare a public field in a MonoBehaviour, it appears in the Inspector for that component. For UI, expose references such as TextMeshProUGUI and Image so you can assign scene objects directly. This explicit connection is robust and designer-friendly. To wire an element, select the GameObject with your script, then drag the UI element from the Hierarchy into the appropriate public field slot in the Inspector. If a field is null at runtime, the script will safely check for null before updating visuals — add null checks to avoid errors. A practical example: drag ScoreText into scoreText and HealthBarFill into healthBarFill for the UIManager. Avoid using runtime object searches such as GameObject. Find which are brittle and slow. A common misconception is that private fields cannot be set in Inspector; you can use [SerializeField] to keep a field private but visible in the Inspector. Key takeaway: prefer explicit Inspector wiring for UI references, add null checks, and document which fields designers should assign. What documentation would you add to clarify required Inspector assignments?

keyIdea.title: Inspector wiring
keyIdea.text: Expose UI references as public or serialized fields and drag scene objects into them to connect visuals to script logic.

content.html:
Architecture
Inspector & Wiring
Expose UI references, assign them in Inspector, and add null checks in code.
Public Fields: Visible and editable in Inspector.
[SerializeField] Private: Keeps encapsulation but still assignable in Editor.
Null Checks: Prevent runtime errors if a reference is left unset during testing.
Practical Example
Select UIManager in the Hierarchy and drag the ScoreText object into the scoreText field. Repeat for HealthBarFill. Run the scene and press P/O to verify updates.
Pro tip: annotate scripts with a small header comment describing which fields must be set in the Inspector for designers.
Common Mistake

Leaving references unassigned and then relying on runtime searches leads to fragile scenes.

screens.title: Testing & Resolution Behavior
screens.subtitle: How anchors and canvas settings affect different screen sizes

narration.text: Testing UI across resolutions is essential. The Game view resolution dropdown lets you simulate different screen sizes and aspect ratios. Compare two approaches: fixed offsets with static anchors versus proper anchors or stretch presets. Fixed offsets look right on one resolution but will drift on others. Anchored elements remain in their intended corners or stretch appropriately. For example, a top-right score anchored to the top-right corner maintains a consistent margin on both a 16:9 monitor and a 9:16 phone screen. Another consideration is the Canvas Scaler component on the Canvas: settings like Scale With Screen Size influence how UI scales; choose a reference resolution and a match setting to control scaling across devices. A typical misconception is to rely on the Editor window alone; always test with multiple Game view presets. Key takeaway: simulate target devices, use anchors and Canvas Scaler to achieve consistent results, and keep interactive areas sufficiently large for touch screens. Which device sizes will you include in your test list? Testing & Resolution Behavior means use game view presets and canvas scaler settings plus anchors to verify ui across resolutions and input types.. In practical terms, how anchors and canvas settings affect different screen sizes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Test early and often
keyIdea.text: Use Game view presets and Canvas Scaler settings plus anchors to verify UI across resolutions and input types.

content.html:
Comparison
Fixed Offsets vs Anchors
Fixed offsets can break on different aspect ratios; anchors express intended behavior across sizes.
Anchored: Maintains margin from corner regardless of resolution.
Fixed Offset: Looks correct on one resolution but drifts on others.
Canvas Scaler
Set Reference Resolution and Screen Match Mode to control how UI elements scale between small and large devices.
Tip: test with a phone, tablet, and desktop preset to ensure touch targets and text remain readable.
Key Takeaway

Simulate target devices and tune anchors plus Canvas Scaler to keep UI consistent and accessible.

screens.title: Event System and Input Handling
screens.subtitle: How Unity routes clicks, hovers and drags to UI elements

narration.text: Unity's Event System is the runtime component that dispatches input events like clicks, pointer movement, and drags to UI elements. When you add UI through the GameObject menu, Unity automatically creates an EventSystem in the scene. UI components such as Button or Toggle rely on the EventSystem to receive On Click and other events. A concrete example: a Button's On Click is dispatched by the EventSystem when a pointer press and release occur within the button area. For keyboard or gamepad navigation, add a Standalone Input Module or an Input System module depending on your input backend. A common misconception is to assume clicks won't register if a Canvas is disabled or behind a blocking object; ensure Canvas and its Graphic Raycaster are enabled and no transparent overlays capture input. Key takeaway: the Event System bridges input sources to UI components; verify its presence and the correct input module in your scene when UI interactions fail. What happens when a full-screen transparent panel blocks your clicks? Event System and Input Handling means the event system routes user inputs to ui components; ensure a proper input module and enabled graphic raycaster are present.. In practical terms, how unity routes clicks, hovers and drags to ui elements. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Event routing
keyIdea.text: The Event System routes user inputs to UI components; ensure a proper input module and enabled Graphic Raycaster are present.

content.html:
Definition
Event System
It dispatches clicks, drags and pointer events to UI elements and requires an input module suited to your input setup.
Graphic Raycaster: Component on Canvas that allows it to receive pointer events.
Input Module: Standalone Input Module or Input System module handles device input mapping.
Troubleshooting
  • Ensure EventSystem exists. If missing, add one via GameObject > UI > Event System.
  • Check for blocking panels with Raycast Target enabled that might capture clicks unintentionally.
  • Verify the correct input module is active for keyboard, mouse, or gamepad support.
Key Takeaway

If UI doesn't respond, check EventSystem, Graphic Raycaster, and overlapping objects that can block input.

screens.title: Common Mistakes, Pro Tips and Next Steps
screens.subtitle: Avoid pitfalls and make a list of improvements you can apply

narration.text: This final lesson slide collects common mistakes and practical tips you can use to improve your UI. Mistakes: not setting anchors and relying on fixed positions, forgetting to set Image Type to Filled for dynamic bars, using GameObject. Find in Start which creates fragile dependencies, and leaving EventSystem out of the scene so buttons are unresponsive. Pro tips: always test with Game view presets for different aspect ratios, use TextMeshPro for improved text rendering, combine Layout Groups with anchors to manage dynamic lists, and document required Inspector fields with comments in your script. For performance, avoid unnecessarily large canvases that frequently rebuild; place dynamic elements on smaller child canvases to reduce redraw cost. Next steps: add simple easing when the health value changes to make updates feel smooth, and create a pause menu using the same Canvas but a different panel that toggles active state. Key takeaway: focus on anchors, explicit wiring, and testing across devices — small changes early save a lot of time later. Which pro tip will you apply first? Common Mistakes, Pro Tips and Next Steps means test across devices, use textmeshpro, wire fields explicitly, avoid runtime searches, and optimize canvas redraws.. In practical terms, avoid pitfalls and make a list of improvements you can apply. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Ship-ready UI habits
keyIdea.text: Test across devices, use TextMeshPro, wire fields explicitly, avoid runtime searches, and optimize canvas redraws.

content.html:
Checklist
  • Set anchors before styling elements.
  • Use Image Type = Filled for bars controlled by scripts.
  • Assign UI references in Inspector; avoid GameObject.Find.
  • Ensure EventSystem and Graphic Raycaster are present.
Pro Tips
Split dynamic UI into smaller canvases to reduce redraw overhead.
Use easing when updating bars for a polished feel.
Document required Inspector fields in the script header for teammates.
Key Takeaway

Avoid common layout mistakes by testing early, wiring explicitly, and optimizing canvases for better runtime performance.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Core terms and their concise meaning

narration.text: Let's summarize the most important terms so you can recall them quickly. Canvas: the container for all UI elements and the place to set render mode preferences. Rect Transform: the UI-specific transform that exposes anchors, pivot and size delta to control 2D layout precisely. Anchors: the four points that determine how a UI element's rectangle relates to its parent, which is essential for responsive designs. Layout Groups: components that automatically arrange child UI elements in rows, columns or grids to simplify dynamic lists. Event System: the runtime bridge between input devices and UI components, required for click and pointer interactions. Keep these short definitions in mind when building interfaces: they describe where UI lives, how it sizes, how it adapts to screens, how lists are organized, and how input flows. screens.subtitle: Three final reminders for robust interfaces

narration.text: Finish with three quick reminders that make a big difference. First: anchors — set them intentionally to express how elements should move or stretch. Second: inspector wiring — expose and assign UI references instead of searching at runtime, and add null checks. Third: test across resolutions — use Game view presets and the Canvas Scaler to ensure readability and correct interaction sizes. These three practices protect your UI from common breakage and make it easier for teammates to iterate.
